title: America's GLP-1 Drug Use Surges as Semaglutide Dominates and Costs Climb
excerpt: A new study finds GLP-1 receptor agonist use grew by 230% among diabetics and 643% among non-diabetics between 2017 and 2022, with semaglutide driving the boom — but total per-person spending is rising even as out-of-pocket costs fall.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • GLP-1 drug use surged 230% among diabetics and 643% among non-diabetics from 2017 to 2022.
  • Semaglutide now represents 54% of GLP-1 prescriptions for diabetics and 65% for non-diabetics.
  • Despite lower out-of-pocket costs, total annual payments per user rose to nearly $7,000.
  • Insurance coverage for GLP-1 drugs remains limited, affecting long-term treatment effectiveness.
  • The GLP-1 surge is significant for the Indian American community facing high diabetes risks.

  • GLP-1 drug use in the US grew 230% among people with diabetes and 643% among those without between 2017 and 2022, according to a study in the Journal of the American Heart Association.
  • Semaglutide now accounts for 54% of GLP-1 prescriptions among diabetics and 65% among non-diabetics, up from single digits in 2018.
  • While patient out-of-pocket costs dropped, total annual payments per user rose to nearly $7,000 — raising questions about long-term affordability for insurers and the healthcare system.

The United States is in the grip of a GLP-1 revolution. A nationally representative study published this week in the Journal of the American Heart Association reveals that use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists surged dramatically between 2017 and 2022, with semaglutide — the molecule behind Ozempic and Wegovy — emerging as the overwhelming driver of growth.

Among Americans with diabetes, GLP-1 use rose 230%, from an estimated 1.5 million users to 5.1 million. Among those without a diabetes diagnosis, adoption exploded by 643%, climbing from 115,000 to 855,000 users, according to the study's analysis of Medical Expenditure Panel Survey data.

Semaglutide Takes Over the Market

The shift within the GLP-1 class has been stark. In 2018, semaglutide accounted for just 10% of GLP-1 users with diabetes and 8% of those without. By 2022, those shares had surged to 54% and 65%, respectively. Liraglutide, once the dominant player, saw its share among diabetics collapse from 42% to 12%.

The turning point came in 2021, when the FDA approved Novo Nordisk's Wegovy for obesity treatment after trials showed users lost an average of 15% of their body weight over 16 months.

"Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple G" injectable targeting three hormones, is expected to seek FDA clearance this year."

A separate Gallup survey from June 2026 found that 11% of US adults now take GLP-1 drugs for weight loss, up from 3% in 2024 — a near quadrupling in two years, according to the New York Post.

The Cost Paradox

The study's financial findings tell a split story. Mean annual out-of-pocket payments fell — from $414 to $252 for patients with diabetes, and from $212 to $157 for those without. Patients are paying less at the pharmacy counter.

But mean total annual payments per user, including insurance, Medicare, and Medicaid contributions, rose from $4,936 to $6,722 for diabetics and from $2,651 to $6,811 for non-diabetics. For non-diabetic semaglutide users specifically, the annual total hit $7,588 in 2022.

"The ICER report shows that GLP-1s, at the cost that they are currently being sold, provide tremendous value to society. But the impact they create on the budget is still massive."

— Sujith Ramachandran, Associate Professor of Pharmacy Administration, University of Mississippi

The Institute for Clinical and Economic Review has found GLP-1s cost-effective — meaning their health benefits justify the price. But as Ramachandran noted in the Journal of Managed Care and Specialty Pharmacy, cost-effective does not mean cost-saving. With 40% of Americans classified as obese, even a fraction seeking treatment could push insurers past the $821 million budget-impact threshold ICER uses as a benchmark.

Insurance Coverage Remains Patchy

Many insurance plans continue to limit GLP-1 coverage to six months or a year for weight management. Patients who stop frequently regain lost weight, undermining long-term health gains. Researchers argue insurers should also provide access to dietitians, fitness programs, and behavioral support — replicating the lifestyle interventions that made GLP-1s effective in clinical trials.

The affordability gap has pushed some patients toward compounded versions of semaglutide and tirzepatide, which are not FDA-approved. The Gallup data showed cost and coverage issues were the primary reasons people switched from brand-name to compounded GLP-1s. The FDA has issued warning letters about compounded versions sold with unapproved or incorrect ingredients.

A Pipeline That Keeps Growing

The FDA approved an oral version of Wegovy in December 2025, and Eli Lilly's oral competitor orforglipron, branded Foundayo, won approval in April 2026. Eli Lilly's retatrutide, a "triple G" injectable targeting three hormones, is expected to seek FDA clearance this year. Beyond obesity and diabetes, GLP-1s are now approved for cardiovascular risk reduction, sleep apnea, kidney disease, and liver disease, with studies ongoing for Alzheimer's disease and substance use disorders.

What It Means for Indian Americans

The GLP-1 surge carries particular relevance for the Indian diaspora. South Asians face elevated risks of Type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, often at lower body mass indexes than other populations. With the US obesity rate declining from a peak of 39.9% in 2022 to 36.4% in 2026, GLP-1 drugs could become an increasingly important tool for a community disproportionately affected by metabolic conditions — provided insurance coverage and affordability hurdles are addressed.
